correctness.rationale: The projective-plane incidence axioms give exactly 24 universal uncoloured rank-one ordered-triple types: 1 all-equal, 9 exactly-two-equal, 2 distinct same-side geometry types and 12 mixed-side types. The proof verifies the required fourth-vertex adjacency masks, with sharp q>=2 witness inequalities q-1>=1 and q(q-1)-1>=1, including equality extensions. The available triple profiles yield exactly four universal rank-two pair types (equality, adjacency, same-side nonadjacency, opposite-side nonadjacency), and every vertex extends to all four, forcing one rank-three singleton type and one rank-four empty type for every finite projective plane. The rank-five four-neighbor sentence distinguishes degrees three and four. Naming point and line sorts yields universal rank-three types but a rank-four concurrent-three-lines/off-union witness, using the exact count q(q-2). A standalone exact rank-type calculation over the 14/26-vertex examples corroborates the finite boundary. No finite test is invoked as an infinite/universal proof.

value.rationale: Quantifier-rank visibility of geometric order is a natural descriptive-complexity invariant for incidence structures; the finding gives a uniform statement over the complete class of finite projective planes, including non-Desarguesian examples, not an arbitrary finite graph census. The four-round extension-profile theorem identifies a precise locality obstruction and the Fano/ternary sharp pair. The one-rank shift when point and line sorts are named demonstrates substantive vocabulary sensitivity: the connected graph has an intrinsic bipartition up to exchange, but the absence of named sorts changes bounded-depth expressibility. The result is a structural, reusable EF lemma rather than a routine calculation of graph degree or reindexing of a known formula.
